extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (epistemology, metaphysics, ethics); educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the nature, limits, and practical effects of reason: how mathematical and empirical evidence arise, what constitutes explanation, the sources of error, and the ethical implications (Stoicism) of practical reason. Aimed at understanding method and limits of science and philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical evidence rests on immediate a priori perception
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidence of mathematics rests essentially not upon demonstration, but upon immediate perception which is a priori and therefore independent of experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstration (logical proof) is often foreign to the matter and does not add to the immediate conviction provided by a priori perception; mathematics' advantage is that its formal element is given as a whole and thus allows proceeding from cause to effect with necessity (e.g., equality of sides known from equality of angles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical knowledge is inductive (consequent→reason) and not unconditionally certain
rubrics_metrics.description: All knowledge through sense-perception and most empirical science proceeds from the consequent to the reason (induction), and therefore lacks unconditional certainty because the same consequent may arise from different reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Induction (from many consequents to one reason) approaches but does not attain mathematical necessity; repeated confirmation can make induction practically reliable, but the possibility of mistake remains (e.g., rare anatomical exceptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Certainty in natural science requires experiments proceeding cause→effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Only in purposely arranged experiments, where knowledge proceeds from the cause to the effect, does the method afford certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such experiments are themselves motivated by hypotheses; natural sciences generally grow by collected and compared experience over centuries rather than being discovered at once as in mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error = illicit inference from consequent to reason (overgeneralisation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every error is an inference from the consequent to the reason that is valid only when the consequent cannot have any other cause; error commonly arises from falsely generalising a particular cause as 'always' the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid error one should recognize limits of induction and prefer 'sometimes' or 'generally' instead of absolute 'always' unless complete induction has been made; examples illustrate how haste or insufficient knowledge produce such false generalisations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation must establish relations according to the principle of sufficient reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanation is the establishment of relations of phenomena to each other according to the applicable form of the principle of sufficient reason; it cannot go further than showing such relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explanation reaches a relation of which no further 'why' can be demanded (e.g., 2+2=4, geometrical truths), asking 'why' is misplaced; valid scientific explanation is relative and shows how phenomena stand to each other under the relevant form of the principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory limits: explanations in science terminate at a qualitas occulta
rubrics_metrics.description: Every explanation in natural science must ultimately end with a 'qualitas occulta'—an originally given quality (e.g., weight, cohesion, life) that cannot be further explained by the principle of sufficient reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two things are ultimately inexplicable: (1) the principle of sufficient reason itself in its forms, and (2) the thing-in-itself (the original source of phenomena). Science must accept such presupposed qualities as limits of its explanatory reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy presupposes nothing and treats everything (including principles) as problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy does not presuppose foundational principles but treats even the principle of sufficient reason and phenomena themselves as problems; it therefore begins where empirical science and its method of explanation end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophy cannot be constructed ex nihilo from firmer principles via demonstration (contra Spinoza); it must handle all items as equally external and to be analysed rather than accepted as prior foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical method: abstraction and unification (know the one in the many)
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy must reproduce the manifold of the world in abstract concepts—presenting the whole in a few general judgements by uniting what is essentially identical in one concept and relegating differences to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid losing itself among particulars, philosophy must use abstraction; the first judgments require the whole to be present (a complete recapitulation), and the mutual harmony of judgments can serve only as confirmation, not as their ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical reason: reason as guide of action is reflective and distinct from moral worth
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason, as practical, enables humans to live a second, abstract life—deliberating about past, future, and possible states—and so to guide action by abstract concepts; however, rational action is distinct from virtuous (moral) action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason can enable consistent, methodical pursuit of ends (good or bad) because it is receptive and not spontaneous; Schopenhauer rejects Kant’s claim that practical reason is the immediate source of virtue and notes that reason can serve both noble and evil maxims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stoic ethical criteria: aim for happiness via ataraxia using reason and virtue as means
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoic ethics develop practical reason to attain happiness understood as peace of mind (ataraxia); virtue is treated as the means to secure inward peace rather than as an end in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stoics advise distinguishing what depends on us (the will) from what does not, live in harmony with oneself (and, for some Stoics, with nature), lower claims/desires relative to what is received, and cultivate knowledge of life's transitory nature to avoid being surprised and losing self-command.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce illusion/error by convergent sensory or evidential support
rubrics_metrics.description: Illusion (deception of the senses) and error (deception of reason) are analogous; multiple sense impressions pointing to the same cause reduce the possibility of illusion, though even all senses may be deceived in rare cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, require corroboration across senses or independent lines of evidence; be aware that counterfeit or exceptional cases can still mislead, so convergence reduces but does not eliminate error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-being depends on proportion between desires and possessions (manage expectations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness depends on the proportion between our claims (desires/expectations) and what we receive; suffering arises when expectations exceed what we obtain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One can attain peace either by reducing desires/claims or by increasing what is received; Stoic practice emphasizes correcting expectations through fuller insight into the transitory, contingent nature of worldly goods.
